title: Toltec
capsule: The Toltec were a Mesoamerican civilisation centred on Tula (Tollan) in the modern state of Hidalgo, Mexico, which emerged from a fusion of Nonoalca migrants from the Gulf Coast and Chichimec groups from the north, and dominated the central Mexican highlands during the Early Postclassic period (c.950–1150 CE). At its peak Tula Grande covered approximately sixteen square kilometres and housed an estimated 60,000 inhabitants, famous for monumental colonnaded halls, stepped pyramids, and the colossal Atlantean warrior columns atop Pyramid B. The Aztecs later idealised the Toltecs as the epitome of civilisation and artistic mastery — their language, Nahuatl, coined the word tōltēkatl to mean skilled artisan — though modern scholarship debates how much Aztec tradition reflects political mythology rather than history. Tula was sacked and burned around 1150–1200 CE by advancing Chichimec peoples, ending the city's political primacy.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The spatial extent of Toltec political authority is poorly attested and contested; the city of Tula itself is archaeologically well documented, but the reach of its hegemony beyond the central Mexican highlands rests on indirect ceramic and iconographic evidence.
